patient_actor_hidden.History: Patient reports sudden, painless loss of vision in her right eye that occurred about 30 minutes ago. She mentions the episode happened while she was watching TV. On further questioning, she reports a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She admits to not always adhering to her prescribed medication regimen.

Symptoms.Primary_Symptom: Sudden, painless loss of vision in the right eye
Secondary_Symptoms: No changes in vision in the left eye
No recent history of eye trauma

patient_actor_hidden.Past_Medical_History: Coronary artery disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus.
patient_actor_hidden.Social_History: Patient lives alone and is recently retired. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol occasionally.
patient_actor_hidden.Review_of_Systems: Denies recent headache, dizziness, chest pain, or difficulty breathing.

objective_for_doctor: Assess and manage a patient presenting with sudden, unilateral loss of vision.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?
“My right eye’s vision suddenly went away about 30 minutes ago. It was painless and happened while I was watching TV, and my left eye is unchanged.”
Can you tell me if you noticed any other symptoms with the vision loss, such as flashes of light, floaters, or a curtain‑like shadow over part of your visual field?
“I didn’t notice any flashes of light or floaters, but it felt like a curtain came down over part of my visual field in the right eye.” “I haven’t had any eye pain or redness either.”
Do you have any known medical conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, heart disease, or a history of smoking?

“I do have high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, and I’ve also been told I have coronary artery disease.” “I smoke about 10 cigarettes a day, and I don’t always take my prescribed medications as I should.”
Can you describe what you can still see with that eye—are you able to perceive any light, shapes, or colors, or is it completely dark?
“It’s not completely dark—I can still make out some light and vague shapes, but the vision is very blurred and I can’t see clearly through that curtain area in my right eye.”
Do you have any associated symptoms such as headache, scalp tenderness
“No, I don’t have a headache or scalp tenderness, and I haven’t had dizziness either.” “I haven’t had chest pain or trouble breathing, either.”
Are you able to see any movement of your right eye (e.g., the eye looks “shut” or deviated), or does it move normally when you look in different directions?
“I think my right eye moves normally when I look around, and it doesn’t look shut or deviated—I don’t notice any difference in eye position, just the vision issue with that curtain area.”
Do you notice any difference in the way the pupils react—specifically, does the right pupil respond less briskly to light compared with the left (a relative afferent pupillary defect)?

“Doctor, I haven’t really checked my pupils in a mirror or noticed a difference in how they react to light compared with the left eye.” “I can’t tell if the right pupil responds less briskly, but the main thing I’m aware of is that the curtain-like area in my right vision is very blurred and I can’t see clearly through it.”
On a scale of 20/20, how well can you see with your right eye right now? For example, are you able to read normal print, see faces, or is it markedly reduced?

“Right now I can’t read normal print with my right eye, and faces look very blurry—there’s a curtain-like area where things aren’t clear at all, though I can still detect some light and vague shapes.”
When a light is shone into your right eye, does the left pupil constrict normally (i.e., do you notice a difference in the light reflex between the two eyes)?

“I’m not sure—I haven’t noticed a difference between the pupils when light is shone, and I haven’t been checking them closely.” “If you shine a light, I’ll tell you whether I notice one pupil responding less briskly than the other.”
Since the vision loss began about 30 minutes ago, has it stayed the same, gotten better, or gotten worse in the meantime?
“It’s stayed about the same since it started—if anything, it might be slightly worse, but I haven’t noticed it getting clearly better.”

Is the loss affecting your entire right visual field (you can’t see anything at all with that eye), or is it limited to a particular portion—such as the upper half, lower half, or peripheral “curtain” while central vision remains relatively better?

“It’s limited to a particular portion—I’d describe it as a curtain covering part of the field, not the entire right vision. My central vision is also quite blurred, but I can still detect some light and vague shapes through the affected area.”
How old are you?
“I’m 60 years old. I noticed the curtain-like blurred area in my right vision started about 30 minutes ago and it’s stayed about the same, maybe slightly worse, and it’s not completely dark.”
[DDX] Retinal detachment, Central retinal artery occlusion, Central retinal vein occlusion, Non‑arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, Vitreous hemorrhage
